Saying 'I'm a layperson when it comes to cars' is a casual, humble way to admit you don't know something.

distinctions.note: Layman is gendered and older; Americans now prefer layperson or laypeople in most contexts.
Amateur implies lower skill, while layperson simply means not an expert or not clergy.

examples.everyday: I'm a layperson when it comes to cars, so I'll trust your mechanic's advice.
examples.professional: The report needs to be readable by a layperson, not just by the statisticians on the team.
examples.analytical: Luther's doctrine of the priesthood of all believers gave the layperson a dignity that the medieval hierarchy had largely withheld.

nuance.analogy: Like a visitor standing in a museum with no art training, able to enjoy the paintings but not to judge their technique.
nuance.etymology: From 'lay', from Greek laikos (of the people), via Latin laicus, plus 'person'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable 'PER' with a full vowel; it is reduced to an r-colored schwa.
Assuming 'layperson' means someone unqualified or foolish; in theology and technical writing it is a neutral term.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word laos (λαός) means 'people,' and the church's word 'laity' comes from it. Scripture applies priestly language to the whole people of God: 1 Peter 2:5 calls believers a holy priesthood, and 1 Peter 2:9 calls them a royal priesthood and God's own people.

traditions.view: The laity are the baptized people of God who are not ordained, and they take an active part in worship, the Eucharist, and the life of the church, which is understood as the whole people, laos.
The lay faithful are the baptized who are not in holy orders, and canon law distinguishes them from clerics; the Second Vatican Council stressed their vocation to sanctify the world.

Most Protestants teach the priesthood of all believers and reject a sharp sacred-secular divide, though Lutheran and Reformed churches still separate ordained ministers from laypeople, while many free churches stress lay ministry.

senses.definition: Having the shape of a leaf.

core.definition: Having the shape of a leaf, usually flat, with a pointed or rounded tip and a narrow base.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound adjective the first element, LEEF, usually carries the main stress, as with 'heart-shaped'. The ending 'shaped' is pronounced /ʃeɪpt/, with a final t sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is common in design, botany and jewelry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'leaf-shaped' to describe objects such as pendants, cookies, pastry, tiles and windows, and in botany to describe plant parts. It is a simple descriptive compound rather than a formal term. For a more precise botanical term, scientists may use 'lanceolate' or 'ovate'.

distinctions.note: Leafy means having many leaves, while leaf-shaped means having the form of a leaf.
Heart-shaped describes a specific familiar form, while leaf-shaped covers many oval or pointed forms of leaves.

examples.everyday: Grandma's silver necklace has a small leaf-shaped pendant that she wears on Sundays.
examples.professional: The new logo uses a leaf-shaped icon, so we need a version that still reads clearly at sixteen pixels.
examples.analytical: Many plant organs are leaf-shaped, which suggests that similar developmental constraints shape their outlines across different species.

nuance.analogy: A leaf-shaped object is like a cookie cutter that has been pressed into the form of a leaf.
nuance.etymology: Compound of leaf (from Old English lēaf) and shaped, from shape (from Old English gesceap).
common_mistakes: Stressing 'shaped' as the main word; in American speech the first element usually carries the main stress.
Confusing 'leaf-shaped' with 'leafy', which describes many leaves rather than a shape.

senses.definition: (obsolete) Slowness; sluggishness.
senses.example: lentitude of temperament
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: Slowness or sluggishness in movement, action, or thought; a lack of speed or energy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowels are weak. Say 'LEN-tuh-tood,' and keep the final syllable as a long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it describes sluggishness in a somewhat dry, literary way and can sound slightly pretentious in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'lentitude' outside of formal writing, literature, or vocabulary-focused contexts. In everyday speech they say 'sluggishness,' 'slowness,' or 'lethargy' instead. It can be useful when writing precise or elegant prose about a slow process.

distinctions.note: Lentitude is more formal and literary, while sluggishness is the common everyday word for slowness in people or systems.
Lethargy implies tiredness or lack of energy, while lentitude refers more simply to slowness of movement or change.

examples.everyday: After the long flight, I could feel a kind of lentitude settle into my legs.
examples.professional: The project's lentitude frustrated the team, so we added a weekly checkpoint to speed decisions.
examples.analytical: The author's prose has a deliberate lentitude that mirrors the slow, reflective pace of the narrator's memory.

nuance.analogy: Lentitude is like a river moving through a flat valley: the water still flows, but it barely seems to move.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin lentitudo, from Latin lentus, meaning 'slow' or 'pliant.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'lentil' because of the shared start; the words are unrelated.
Using it in casual conversation where 'slowness' or 'sluggishness' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: A person who frees or liberates.

core.definition: A person or group that frees people or places from oppression, captivity or control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LIB. The final -or is a reduced 'er,' and the t between vowels is a flap, so it sounds close to 'd.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It honors someone who freed others, but it may sound grandiose when used of a minor helper.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use liberator for historical or political figures, such as soldiers who ended an occupation or activists who freed people from captivity. In everyday speech you would more likely say rescuer, hero or savior. Calling a friend your liberator is a warm but dramatic joke.

distinctions.note: A rescuer saves someone from immediate danger, such as a drowning swimmer. A liberator frees people from longer-term oppression or captivity.
Emancipator is more specific and usually refers to someone who freed enslaved people or gave legal independence. Liberator is broader.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still calls the soldiers who arrived in his village in 1945 liberators.
examples.professional: The campaign positions the mobile app as a liberator for small farmers who were locked into high-fee lending.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly presents God as a liberator who acts in history on behalf of the oppressed.

nuance.analogy: A liberator is like the person who unlocks a cell door from outside, while the prisoner walks out under their own power.
nuance.etymology: From liberate plus the agent suffix -or, from Latin liberator, 'one who frees.'
common_mistakes: Using liberator for a rescuer in an everyday emergency, which sounds too grand.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'or' vowel instead of the reduced 'er.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word yasha' means to save, deliver or give rescue, and the Greek lytrōtēs (deliverer or redeemer) is used in Acts for Moses. In Judges 3:9, God raises up a deliverer for Israel, and in Exodus 3:8 God says he has come down to deliver the people from Egypt. Acts 7:35 applies the idea of a deliverer to Moses as God's chosen agent of liberation.

liberator.etymology: From Latin *līberātor* (“one who sets free”), from *līberāre*, past participle *līberātus* (“to set free”); see liberate.

senses.definition: In a licit manner, legally, in a manner compatible with law.
senses.example: The company could not licitly sell the software without the proper federal permits.

core.definition: In a way that is legal or permitted by law or rules.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, LIS. The middle syllable is a reduced 'it', and the word has no long 'i' like 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes legal or rule-compliant conduct without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: This is a formal word used mostly by lawyers, regulators, compliance staff, and writers. Americans would normally say 'legally' or 'legitimately' in everyday speech. The adjective 'licit' is also rare, so the adverb is even rarer.

distinctions.note: Legally is the everyday word and refers to statute; licitly can also mean permitted by rules or custom.
Legitimately often means genuinely or fairly, not only lawful; licitly is narrower and more technical.

examples.everyday: I want to be sure those tickets were bought licitly, not from some scalper.
examples.professional: Please confirm that every training dataset was licitly obtained before we publish the model.
examples.analytical: Whether the transfer was conducted licitly turns on the statute's definition of consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt stamped by the official office: the act is recognized as allowed by the rules.
nuance.etymology: From Latin licitus, past participle of licere 'to be permitted'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'lie' (/laɪ/) instead of /lɪs/.
Using it in casual speech where 'legally' is the natural choice.

senses.definition: Synonym of life jacket.
senses.example: Every passenger must wear a life vest while the small boat crosses the rough lake.

core.definition: A buoyant, wearable vest that keeps you afloat in water.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VEST, which has a short e as in 'bed'. Do not change it to the long a sound of 'vast'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a safety item that usually suggests a calm, responsible precaution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say life vest for a wearable flotation vest, often on boats, in pools, and in airplane safety demonstrations. It is used more casually than life jacket, which appears more in formal and official safety language. Many Americans use life vest and life jacket interchangeably.

distinctions.note: Life vest and life jacket mean nearly the same thing in everyday American use, though life jacket is more common in official safety language.
A life preserver can be a ring or an older vest, while a life vest is specifically worn on the body.

examples.everyday: Make sure the kids wear their life vests before we get in the kayak, even if the lake looks calm.
examples.professional: All field staff must wear a life vest when working on the dock, and the supervisor will check the equipment each morning.
examples.analytical: The life vest reflects a cultural shift toward preventive safety, where individual protection is built into ordinary activities.

nuance.analogy: A life vest is like a wearable inner tube, keeping your body floating while you rest or wait for help.
nuance.etymology: Life comes from Old English lif; vest comes from French veste, from Italian vesta, meaning a garment.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing vest with the vowel of 'vast'.
Using life vest for a ring that is thrown, which is a life ring.

senses.definition: A major appendage of human or animal, used for locomotion (such as an arm, leg or wing).
senses.example: The surgeon explained that the injured limb might regain full movement with therapy.

senses.definition: A branch of a tree.
The part of the bow, from the handle to the tip.
An elementary piece of the mechanism of a lock.
senses.example: The locksmith replaced a worn limb inside the old deadbolt cylinder.

senses.definition: A thing or person regarded as a part or member of, or attachment to, something else.
senses.example: Our regional office is a limb of the national nonprofit, funded by its donors.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of limb of Satan (“a wicked or mischievous child”).
The graduated edge of a circle or arc.
senses.example: Read the angle where the pointer crosses the limb of the brass protractor.

senses.definition: The apparent visual edge of a celestial body.
senses.example: the solar limb

senses.definition: The border or upper spreading part of a monopetalous corolla, or of a petal or sepal; blade.
senses.example: The orchid's lower petal has a broad limb that curves toward the stamen.

senses.definition: To remove the limbs from (an animal or tree).
senses.example: They limbed the felled trees before cutting them into logs.

senses.definition: To supply with limbs.
senses.example: The sculptor limbed the mannequin carefully before attaching the painted torso.

senses.definition: To thoroughly defeat an opponent in fisticuffs.
senses.example: Brian limbed Roger over at the Beahive last night.

core.definition: A major part of the body that sticks out, such as an arm or a leg, used for moving or grasping; also a large branch of a tree.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'i' like in 'big' and end with a clear m. The b is silent and should not be pronounced, so do not say 'lim-buh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In medical or emergency contexts it is serious, and in idioms like 'out on a limb' it is figurative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'limb' most often in phrases like 'lost a limb' or 'out on a limb', and in tree descriptions such as 'a big limb fell in the storm'. 'Arm' or 'leg' is more common when speaking about a specific body part. The word is a bit formal in everyday talk, so people usually say 'arm' or 'leg' in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Branch' is the usual everyday word for a tree part, while 'limb' is common in tree and forestry contexts and is used more for big, main branches.
'Member' can mean a body part in formal or biblical language, but it is more often used for a person in a group.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog got a bad cut on one of its hind limbs, so we took it to the vet.
examples.professional: The insurance form asks whether the claimant lost any upper or lower limbs in the accident.
examples.analytical: Paul uses the image of the body and its limbs to argue that every member of the church depends on the others.

nuance.analogy: A limb is like a bridge from the trunk to the outside world, carrying weight and movement in both directions.
nuance.etymology: From Old English lim, meaning member or branch of the body.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent b in 'limb' as in 'lamb' with a b sound.
Using 'limb' for a casual body part where 'arm' or 'leg' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word melos means a member or limb of the body. In 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 Paul compares the church to a body with many members, and he says that if one member suffers, all suffer together. Romans 12:4-5 makes a similar point, that many members form one body in Christ and each belongs to the others.

limb.etymology: From Middle English *lyme*, *lim*, from Old English *lim* (“limb, branch”), from **limu*, from Proto-Germanic **limuz* (“branch, limb”).

senses.definition: A liminal point; the threshold of a physiological or psychological response.

core.definition: In psychology, the threshold point at which a stimulus becomes just strong enough to be sensed or to produce a response.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long 'y' sound, and keep the final syllable short like 'men'. It is a Latin-derived word, so do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from psychology and physiology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'limen' outside psychology, physiology and academic writing. In everyday speech people say 'threshold' or 'tipping point'. The word is mainly found in research on perception and sensory response.

distinctions.note: 'Threshold' is a general word for a doorway or boundary, while 'limen' is a technical term for a sensory or psychological boundary.

examples.everyday: That noise was so faint I wasn't sure I heard it, so it must have been near my limen.
examples.professional: Our lab measured the auditory limen for each participant before starting the experiment.
examples.analytical: Fechner's work on the limen established a mathematical relation between stimulus intensity and perceived sensation.

nuance.analogy: The limen is like the minimum volume a speaker must reach before anyone in the room can hear it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin limen, meaning threshold or doorway.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'LIM-en' with a short i, which is not the usual American pronunciation.
Using 'limen' as a general word for any boundary.

senses.definition: An occupation.
senses.example: After college, she chose a line of work that let her help people.

core.definition: The type of job or profession a person does, especially the broad field someone works in.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on WURK, and of reduces to uv. Pronounce the r clearly in the r-colored vowel of work, not the o of wok.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a casual, polite way to ask what someone does for a living.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask What's your line of work? at parties, in waiting rooms, or when getting to know a neighbor, as a softer alternative to What do you do? It is informal but polite. A natural reply names your field, such as I'm in insurance or I'm a nurse, which is more common than giving a job title.

distinctions.note: Job is the everyday word for a specific position. Line of work refers to the broader field or type of work someone does.
Career describes a long path of professional progress over time. Line of work describes the field you are in right now.
Occupation is more formal and common on forms and official documents. Line of work is more casual and conversational.

collocations: in the same line of work
a line of work with long hours

examples.everyday: What's your line of work, if you don't mind me asking?
examples.professional: Most of our interns are moving into data science, though they came from very different lines of work.
examples.analytical: Scholars have argued that a person's identity depends less on their line of work than on the institutions that recognize it.

nuance.analogy: Like a lane on a highway: it is the road you are currently in, even if you can change lanes later.
nuance.etymology: Line from Latin linea; work from Old English weorc.
common_mistakes: Saying line of job or line of profession instead of line of work.
Reversing the order to work line, which sounds unnatural in American English.

senses.definition: Synonym of tongue.
A median process of the labium, at the underside of the mouth in insects, and serving as a tongue.
senses.example: Entomologists examined the lingua of the honeybee, which the insect uses to lap up nectar.

core.definition: Latin word for language or tongue, used in English mainly in the fixed phrase lingua franca and in some technical or anatomical terms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LING-gwuh. The final syllable is a weak schwa, so do not stress it or pronounce it as LING-gwah.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is descriptive and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use lingua alone in everyday speech. They say language, or tongue for the body part. The phrase lingua franca is common in business, travel and academic writing, meaning a shared language used among speakers of different native languages.

distinctions.note: Language is the everyday word, while lingua is a Latin-derived term used mostly in fixed phrases and technical contexts.
Lingo is informal and often means jargon, while lingua is formal and used for language as a general or technical concept.
Tongue is the common word for the organ in the mouth, while lingua is a technical term for the same organ in anatomy.

examples.everyday: At the airport, English became the lingua franca between us, since none of us spoke the same first language.
examples.professional: English serves as the lingua franca of our global engineering team, so every design review is held in English.
examples.analytical: Scholars describe Latin as the lingua franca of medieval Europe, a shared medium that crossed political borders.

nuance.analogy: A lingua franca is like a common currency for speech: each person carries their own coins, but everyone accepts one currency for exchange.
nuance.etymology: Latin lingua, meaning tongue or language.
common_mistakes: Using lingua alone as a general word for language in everyday conversation, where language is the natural word.
Pronouncing lingua franca with broad vowels such as LING-gwah FRAN-kah instead of LING-gwuh FRANG-kuh.

senses.definition: The process of being, or state of having been, made liquid (from either a solid or a gas).
The liquid or semiliquid that results from this process.

core.definition: The process of turning a solid or a gas into a liquid, or the state of having become liquid.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -fak- syllable. The 'qu' is pronounced 'kw', and the ending -tion is pronounced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use liquefaction mainly in science, engineering and geology. Soil liquefaction during earthquakes is a common topic in California and other places with seismic risk. In everyday talk, people say 'turning into liquid' or 'melting' instead.

distinctions.note: Melting usually means a solid becoming liquid through heat, while liquefaction also covers gases and the soil-liquefaction effect caused by shaking.
Dissolution means one substance spreading through another, usually a solid in a liquid, while liquefaction means becoming a liquid itself.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the houses by the river could have problems with liquefaction if there's a big earthquake.
examples.professional: Our geotechnical team flagged liquefaction risk at two sites for the new substation.
examples.analytical: The liquefaction of saturated sediment under shaking shows how a seemingly stable foundation can suddenly behave like a fluid.

nuance.analogy: Liquefaction is like a sandcastle turning into soup when the water rises beneath it.
nuance.etymology: From liquefy plus -action, from Latin liquefacere, 'to make liquid'.
common_mistakes: Placing the main stress on the first syllable, as in 'LIK-wuh-fak-shun'.
Pronouncing the qu as 'k' and dropping the w sound.

liquefaction.etymology: From Middle English *liquefaction*, from Middle French *liquefaction*, from *liquefactiō*.

senses.definition: The condition of being literal.

core.definition: The quality of being literal: following the exact, plain meaning of words rather than their figurative or metaphorical sense.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the -AL- syllable (the vowel of 'cat'), with a weaker secondary stress on LIT. The unstressed vowels reduce to uh, and the t between vowels is a flap that sounds close to a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a quality, and it can be praise (precision) or criticism (rigid, unimaginative reading) depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use literality in conversation; they say literalness or simply 'the literal meaning.' You will meet it mostly in philosophy, translation studies, hermeneutics and academic writing. In speech, 'taking things too literally' is the natural phrase.

distinctions.note: Literalness is the everyday and more common word for the same quality; literality is rarer and sounds more technical or philosophical.
Literacy means the ability to read and write; literality means the quality of taking words in their exact sense. The two look similar but are unrelated in meaning.

examples.professional: The spec's literality makes it easy to implement, but it leaves no room for judgment calls.
examples.analytical: Derrida's critique unsettles any claim that a text's literality can be fixed independently of its interpretive context.

nuance.analogy: Like a map that marks every road exactly and leaves out the scenic routes the traveler actually wants.
nuance.etymology: From literal (from Latin litteralis, 'of letters', from littera 'letter') plus the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as LIT-er-AL-i-ty; the main stress is on the -AL- syllable.
Confusing literality with literacy, which means the ability to read and write.

senses.definition: The property of being literal.

core.definition: The quality of being literal: taking words in their plain, exact sense without figurative interpretation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIT. The -ness ending is a reduced nuhs, not nes, and the r is clearly pronounced in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can describe useful precision, but it often implies a lack of imagination or humor.
nuance.usage_note: Literalness appears in ordinary English when someone interprets things too strictly, as in 'a child's literalness.' It is more common than literality in American speech and writing. In religious and academic settings it describes a method of reading texts in their plain sense.

distinctions.note: The two mean nearly the same thing; literalness is more common and everyday, while literality is more technical.
Accuracy is about correctness of facts; literalness is about reading words in their strict sense, even when that misses the intended meaning.

examples.everyday: Kids sometimes take sarcasm with a literalness that surprises their parents.
examples.professional: The translation's literalness helps reviewers check the source, though a few sentences read awkwardly.
examples.analytical: Medieval exegetes insisted on the literalness of Scripture's historical narratives while still seeking deeper spiritual meanings.

nuance.analogy: Like a cook who follows a recipe to the gram and never tastes the soup.
nuance.etymology: From literal (from Latin litteralis, 'of letters') plus the suffix -ness, from Old English -nes.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as nes with a full vowel; it is a reduced nuhs.
Confusing literalness with literacy, which means the ability to read and write.

senses.definition: Like or resembling a lizard.
(rare) Like a lizard, in a lizardlike way.
senses.example: The old man crept lizardlike along the sun-warmed stones of the garden wall.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Resembling a lizard in shape, skin, movement or appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle 'ard' is a short, r-colored 'erd' sound. The final 'like' is a secondary stress, not a full weak syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It can describe a person's cold or unpleasant look, or be used neutrally for animals and creatures.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lizardlike' to describe appearance or movement, such as lizardlike skin or quick, lizardlike motions. Some writers hyphenate it as 'lizard-like,' and both forms are accepted. The adverb sense is rare, so use it mainly as an adjective.

distinctions.note: Reptilian refers to the whole group of reptiles and can sound cold or primitive when used about people, while lizardlike points to the lizard's shape or movement.
Snakelike describes long, limbless bodies and sliding motion, while lizardlike suggests four legs, scaly skin and quick darting movements.

examples.everyday: That little dinosaur toy has a lizardlike tail and bumpy green skin that my son loves.
examples.professional: The robot's lizardlike gait made it more stable on the rocky test surface.
examples.analytical: The novelist gives the villain a lizardlike stillness that suggests patience and cold calculation.

nuance.analogy: Like a gecko on a wall, the word describes something with a lizard's shape, scales or quick, darting way of moving.
nuance.etymology: Formed from lizard, from Old French lezard, from Latin lacerta, 'lizard,' plus the suffix -like.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllable as 'lizzard' with a full 'ard' vowel; the American form is 'LIZ-erd.'
Using lizardlike as a noun, as in 'a lizardlike,' which is not standard English.

senses.definition: A wolf.

core.definition: A wolf, especially a Spanish-speaking or Southwestern American term for a gray wolf, used mainly in regional and literary contexts.

pronunciation.tip: Spanish stress falls on the first syllable, LOH-boh, and the final vowel is a clear oh sound, not the bow of a bow tie. Do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In Western and frontier writing it can suggest wildness or danger, as the wolf does in folklore.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, lobo appears mainly in the Southwest, in Spanish-speaking communities, in Western writing and as a nickname, such as the University of New Mexico Lobos. Most Americans say wolf, which is the normal English word. Use lobo when speaking Spanish, discussing New Mexico culture, or describing the Mexican gray wolf in regional contexts.

distinctions.note: Wolf is the standard English word for the animal; lobo is a Spanish loanword used mainly in Southwestern or Spanish-language contexts.
A coyote is a smaller, different canine species with a thinner build; a lobo is a true wolf, larger and heavier.

examples.everyday: Our guide said a lobo pack had been spotted near the trail this spring.
examples.professional: The wildlife biologist's report tracks the Mexican gray wolf, called lobo locally, across the Gila region.
examples.analytical: The Spanish word lobo recalls the frontier past, when the wolf was both a threat to livestock and a symbol of the wild.

nuance.etymology: From Spanish lobo, wolf, from Latin lupus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it LOH-bow, as in low-bow; the final vowel is oh.
Using lobo as a general English word for wolf; in American English, wolf is the normal word.

senses.definition: Credentials: the combination of a user's identification and password used to enter a computer.
senses.example: Using the same logon for different systems can be a security risk.

senses.definition: The process of logging on.
senses.example: The user's desktop is displayed shortly after logon.

core.definition: The user ID and password used to enter a computer system, or the act of entering them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LOG-on, as a noun. The verb 'log on' stresses the second word, as in 'log ON', and the vowel in both syllables is the open American 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a routine technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'login' for websites and apps, and 'logon' more often in Windows, enterprise IT and older documentation. In everyday talk, say 'my login' or 'my password'; use 'logon' when a Windows or IT context calls for it. Both are understood by IT staff.

distinctions.note: Login is the usual spelling for web accounts and everyday talk, while logon is common in Windows and enterprise IT documentation.
A password is only one part of a logon, which also includes a user name or ID.

examples.everyday: Can you help me figure out my logon for the library's public computers?
examples.professional: The helpdesk reset my logon credentials after I was locked out of the network.
examples.analytical: A logon is an authentication event that links a verified identity to a session and opens the system's access controls.

nuance.analogy: Like showing your ID at the door of a members-only club before you can go inside.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb 'log on', where 'log' means to record, from the ship's logbook.
common_mistakes: Writing 'logon' as the verb; the verb is two words, 'log on'.
Using 'logon' for a website sign-in in casual talk, where 'login' is far more common in the US.

senses.definition: Unhappy due to feeling isolated from contact with other people.
Unfrequented by people; desolate.
senses.example: The lonely road wound through empty desert for almost fifty miles without a single house.

senses.definition: Without companions; solitary.
senses.example: After her roommates moved out, she felt lonely in the apartment every evening.

core.definition: Unhappy because you feel cut off from other people, or having few or no companions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, LONE. The second syllable is a light /li/ with a reduced vowel, not a long 'lee'; many learners add an extra syllable here.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing a feeling of sadness. It can be neutral or positive for a quiet place or a chosen solitude, such as 'a lonely road' in a travel story.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lonely constantly in everyday talk, often about feelings: 'I've been feeling lonely since my roommate moved out.' When you want to say a place is empty of people, 'isolated' or 'remote' often sounds more natural than 'lonely'. Saying 'I'm lonely' to a friend is common and not rude, though people sometimes soften it with 'I've been a little lonely lately.'

distinctions.note: Alone describes the physical state of being by yourself and is neutral, while lonely adds a feeling of sadness about it.
Lonesome is more old-fashioned and rural in American English, and it is often used in songs and folk speech.

examples.everyday: I've been feeling kind of lonely since everyone went back to school, so let's grab coffee this weekend.
examples.professional: Several people on the support team told us they feel lonely when working fully remote, so we added weekly video check-ins.
examples.analytical: Camus presents the stranger as lonely not because he is physically alone, but because he cannot share the meaning that others take for granted.

nuance.analogy: Lonely is like an empty room with the lights on: the space is there, but no one is in it.
nuance.etymology: From lone (alone) with the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'lonely' for an empty place where Americans would more often say 'deserted' or 'isolated'.
Confusing 'lonely' with 'alone': 'I am alone tonight' is neutral, while 'I am lonely tonight' expresses sadness.

lonely.etymology: From *lone* + *-ly*, or from an apheretic shortening of *alonely*.

conversation.text: It can get lonely living by yourself in a new city.
My grandpa has been lonely since my grandma passed.
I felt lonely at the party because I didn't know anyone.

core.definition: A title of God in the Hebrew Bible, meaning the LORD who commands the armies, or hosts, of heaven and earth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LORD and HOHSTS, and reduce of to uv. The word hosts ends in a consonant cluster, so do not add a vowel between the s and the t.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent; used in worship and Scripture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear this title in church, Bible readings, and hymns, not in everyday conversation. Use it with reverence in Bible study. Hosts here means armies or assemblies, not party hosts.

distinctions.note: Almighty stresses God's unlimited power; Lord of hosts stresses God's command over armies and heavenly beings.
Lord God is a general title for God; Lord of hosts emphasizes God as commander of the hosts.

collocations: the Lord of hosts is with us
the Lord of hosts has spoken
the Lord of hosts in Isaiah

examples.everyday: Our pastor read a psalm that calls God the Lord of hosts, and the whole congregation sat up straighter.
examples.professional: The sermon drew on Isaiah, so I checked how the Lord of hosts phrase is translated in our study Bible.
examples.analytical: The title Lord of hosts ties Israel's worship to a cosmic command in which God rules over both armies and the heavenly host.

nuance.analogy: Like a general's title that names the whole army he commands, not just one soldier.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew YHWH tseva'ot, where tseva'ot means hosts, armies, or assemblies.
common_mistakes: Thinking hosts means people who throw parties; here it means armies or heavenly beings.
Saying Lord of host in the singular; the Hebrew and English title keeps hosts in the plural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew is YHWH tseva'ot, with tseva'ot meaning hosts, armies, or assemblies, which can refer to Israel's armies or to the heavenly host. Isaiah 6:3 describes the seraphim proclaiming the LORD of hosts holy, with the whole earth full of his glory. Psalm 46:7 says the LORD of hosts is with his people and that the God of Jacob is their refuge. Psalm 24:10 asks who the King of glory is and answers that he is the LORD of hosts.

core.definition: Sunday, the first day of the week, observed by Christians as the day of worship and of Jesus' resurrection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DAY. Pronounce the r clearly in 'Lord's' and end with a z sound, not an s.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear it in church, especially in Reformed, Baptist and Southern traditions. Casual speakers say 'Sunday'. The phrase carries a sense of sacred time.

distinctions.note: Sunday is the ordinary name; Lord's Day stresses its religious meaning.
The Sabbath is the biblical seventh-day rest, which many Christians link to Sunday.
This refers to God's future judgment and victory, not to Sunday.

collocations: the first day of the week

examples.everyday: My grandparents never shopped on the Lord's Day.
examples.professional: The pastor reminded the congregation to gather on the Lord's Day for worship.
examples.analytical: Early Christian writers called Sunday the Lord's Day because it commemorated the resurrection.

nuance.analogy: Sunday seen as a weekly Easter.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kyriake hemera, 'the Lord's day'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the 'Day of the Lord', a different biblical idea.
Dropping the possessive 's.
Using it as an everyday word for Sunday.
nuance.biblical_note: Revelation 1:10 says John was in the Spirit on the Lord's Day (Greek kyriake hemera). Acts 20:7 shows believers gathering on the first day of the week to break bread. 1 Corinthians 16:2 mentions the first day of the week for collecting offerings.

lord's-day.etymology: A Ecclesiastical Latin *diēs Dominicus*, either directly or as a later development of Old Norse *dróttinsdagr* (“Lord's day”)

senses.definition: The state of being loyal; fidelity.
senses.example: brand loyalty

senses.definition: Faithfulness or devotion to some person, cause or nation.
senses.example: He showed loyalty to his local football club after successive relegations.

core.definition: The quality of staying faithful and supportive to a person, group, cause or country, especially when it is tested.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOY, and the middle syllable is reduced to uh before the l. Keep the t clear and say the last syllable as tee, not drop the t.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It names a valued trait, but in business it also has a marketing sense, as in loyalty program.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loyalty about friends, family, sports fans, customers and employees. Loyalty programs and rewards cards are very common in US stores, so the word has a commercial sense too. You can say I appreciate your loyalty in a formal thank-you note or a sales pitch; in casual talk, you might say I'm loyal or I stick with them.

distinctions.note: Allegiance is more formal and usually refers to loyalty to a state, flag or organization; loyalty is more general and personal.
Fidelity is formal and often means faithfulness in a relationship or accuracy in a copy; loyalty is more about support and commitment.

examples.everyday: Her loyalty to her favorite coffee shop is amazing; she goes there every single morning.
examples.professional: We're reviewing the loyalty program to see whether it actually increases repeat purchases.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that loyalty to a local community can conflict with loyalty to universal principles.

nuance.analogy: Like a root system that holds a tree steady in a storm.
nuance.etymology: From loyal (from Old French loial) plus the noun suffix -ty, from Latin legalis, meaning lawful.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as loyality
Using with instead of to, as in loyalty to a person rather than loyalty with a person
Using loyalty as a verb

loyalty.etymology: From Middle English *loialte*, borrowed from Old French *loialte*, *loiauté* (Modern *loyauté*) from *loial* + *-té*, equivalent to *loyal* + *-ty*.

senses.definition: Between warm and cool.
senses.example: Wash it in lukewarm water.

senses.definition: Unenthusiastic (about a proposal or an idea).
senses.example: The suggestion met with only a lukewarm response.

core.definition: Only slightly warm, neither hot nor cold; also, showing little enthusiasm or commitment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on WORM, with a weaker first syllable 'look'. The r in WORM is pronounced, and the vowel is the 'or' sound in 'for'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing temperature. Negative when describing enthusiasm, meaning someone is halfhearted or unimpressed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in everyday life, such as ordering a drink that is 'lukewarm' or complaining that the coffee is not hot enough. It is also common in business, as in 'lukewarm response' or 'lukewarm support'. Pairing it with 'response' or 'reception' sounds very natural.

distinctions.note: Tepid is more formal and usually used for water or bath temperature, while lukewarm is the everyday American word.
Indifferent means not caring at all, while lukewarm suggests mild interest that is not strong enough.

examples.everyday: Could you warm this up? The soup is only lukewarm.
examples.professional: The client gave a lukewarm response to the proposal, so we need to explain the benefits more clearly.
examples.analytical: His lukewarm defense of the policy suggests private doubts that he does not wish to voice publicly.

nuance.analogy: Like a bath that is neither hot enough to relax nor cold enough to shock, and so satisfies no one.
nuance.etymology: From luke 'tepid' (from Middle English) plus warm; the exact origin of luke is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Writing 'luke warm' as two words, which is not standard.
Using it for strong dislike; lukewarm means mild, not hostile.

lukewarm.etymology: From Middle English *leukwarm*, *lukewarm* (“lukewarm, tepid”), equivalent to *luke* + *warm*.

conversation.text: My coffee is lukewarm; could you heat it up?
The soup came out lukewarm, so I asked them to reheat it.
I don't mind cold pizza, but I hate lukewarm food.

senses.definition: Synonym of golden hour (“period of soft daylight shortly after sunrise or before sunset”).

core.definition: The short period just after sunrise or before sunset when the light is soft and warm, favored by photographers and filmmakers.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OW, and the h in hour is silent, so the word begins with the ow sound. The final r is clear in American speech, giving OW-er.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests beauty, warmth and soft light.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use magic hour mainly in photography, film and social media. Many Americans now prefer golden hour for the same time, so either term will be understood. You might say 'Let's go to the lake around magic hour' when planning pictures with friends.

distinctions.note: Golden hour is the more common American term for the same period; magic hour sounds a little more poetic and is used in film.
Blue hour is the dim period when the sun is below the horizon and the sky looks deep blue, so it is not the same as the warm light of magic hour.

examples.everyday: Let's go to the lake around magic hour, the light is perfect for pictures.
examples.professional: Schedule the product photos for magic hour, when the warm light will flatter the packaging without heavy editing.
examples.analytical: Cinematographers prize magic hour because its low, diffuse light reduces harsh contrast, which changes the mood of the scene.

nuance.analogy: Magic hour is like a late-afternoon cup of tea: everything looks softer and warmer for a little while.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the h in hour, as in HOUR-ly with a breathed h; the h is silent.
Thinking magic hour is a fixed sixty minutes; it lasts a limited time that depends on the season and location.

senses.definition: Using pompous speech; speaking with deliberately long or esoteric words.

core.definition: Using grand, pompous or deliberately showy language, with big or unusual words that sound impressive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -NIL-, and keep the first vowel short, as in 'mag'. The final -ent is a reduced syllable, not a full 'ent' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly mocking. It implies that the speaker is more concerned with sounding impressive than with being clear.
nuance.usage_note: This adjective is used mainly in writing, reviews and formal commentary, often to describe a politician, preacher or writer. Americans would normally say 'pompous' or 'full of big words' in casual talk. Calling someone magniloquent in their hearing would be a sharp insult, so save it for careful written criticism.

distinctions.note: Pompous describes a self-important manner in general; magniloquent refers specifically to a grand, showy style of speaking or writing.
Eloquent is a praise word for speech that moves and persuades; magniloquent is a criticism of speech that is more ornate than useful.

examples.everyday: Our new manager gives magniloquent speeches at every meeting, but I still don't know what she wants from us.
examples.professional: The proposal was magniloquent and overlong, so I asked the author to state the recommendation in two plain sentences.
examples.analytical: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address is sometimes praised for being spare, though nineteenth-century orators were often magniloquent in ways modern readers find hard to stomach.

nuance.analogy: A magniloquent speaker is like a tour guide who uses a hundred fancy words to describe a simple garden, so the garden disappears behind the words.
nuance.etymology: From Latin magniloquus, from magnus (great) and loqui (to speak).
common_mistakes: Using magniloquent to mean 'eloquent' as a compliment, when it is usually a criticism.
Mispronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: A temporary (usually insubstantial) substitution.
senses.example: We used a coat hanger as a makeshift until the plumber arrived.

senses.definition: Made to work or suffice; improvised; substituted.
senses.example: They used the ledge and a few branches for a makeshift shelter.

core.definition: Temporary and improvised, used because nothing better is available.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAYK, and shift is lighter. Do not stress the second syllable, and keep the final 'ft' clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it describes something that works for now but is not ideal or permanent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use makeshift for a bed, table, shelter or fix made from whatever is at hand. It is casual and common in everyday talk and in workplace conversations about quick fixes. It can also be used as a noun for a temporary substitute, but the adjective is far more common.

distinctions.note: Temporary describes how long something lasts, while makeshift describes how it was made, as an improvised substitute.
A stopgap fills a gap until something better arrives, while makeshift describes an improvised arrangement that may be rough or clumsy.

examples.everyday: We ate dinner at a makeshift table made from two old crates in the backyard.
examples.professional: The team set up a makeshift fix in the pipeline while the vendor rewrote the parser.
examples.analytical: Many emergency policies are makeshift arrangements that outlast the crisis that justified them.

nuance.analogy: A makeshift fix is like a spare tire: it gets you to the next station, but you should not drive on it for long.
nuance.etymology: From make and shift, in the sense of a way of managing or getting by.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, 'make-SHIFT', instead of MAYK-shift.
Using makeshift as a verb; it is an adjective or noun.

core.definition: A Canaanite royal city in the lowland of Judah, captured by Joshua and the Israelites in the conquest of the land.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, KEH. Pronounce the final vowel as a soft schwa, not 'ah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would use this name in Bible study, sermons, or academic discussion of the conquest narratives. It is a place name rather than a common word, so it appears mainly in religious or scholarly settings.

distinctions.note: Both are cities in the Shephelah region of Judah mentioned in Joshua, but they are separate places.

examples.everyday: Have you read the part of Joshua where the five kings hide in a cave near Makkedah?
examples.professional: In the Sunday school lesson, we'll map Makkedah so the class can see where the southern campaign took place.
examples.analytical: The narrative of the five kings at Makkedah shows Joshua's command over the southern coalition and the fulfillment of the divine promise of conquest.

nuance.analogy: Like a fortified town on a main road in the foothills, Makkedah stood at a strategic point between the coastal plain and the hill country.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MAK-uh-dah'; the stress falls on KEH.
Confusing it with Mekkah or Mecca, which is a different place.
nuance.biblical_note: Makkedah is a Canaanite city in the Shephelah (the lowlands between the coastal plain and the hill country of Judah). In Joshua 10, its king is among the five Amorite kings who form a coalition against Gibeon, and the five kings flee and hide in a cave at Makkedah until Joshua seals it. Joshua 10:28-29 describes Joshua capturing Makkedah and devoting its people to destruction, and Joshua 12:16 lists its king among the defeated kings. Joshua 15:41 places Makkedah among the towns of Judah. The name's Hebrew form (Makkedah) is usually connected with a root meaning 'shepherd' or 'sheepfold', though this derivation is uncertain.

senses.definition: The blundering use of an absurdly inappropriate word or expression in place of a similar-sounding one.
senses.example: The script employed malapropism to great effect.

senses.definition: An instance of such use.
senses.example: The translator matched every malapropism in the original with one from his own language.

core.definition: A funny mistake in which someone uses a word that sounds similar to the correct word but has a very different, wrong meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, MAL. The 'prop' syllable has an open 'ah' vowel, like 'hot,' not 'up,' and the last syllable reduces to 'um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to humorous. It names an error, often with amusement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'malapropism' in discussions of language, literature, and everyday errors. People might say 'That was a malapropism' when someone says 'for all intensive purposes' instead of 'for all intents and purposes.' It is a precise term rather than casual slang, so it fits writing and conversation about language.

distinctions.note: 'Mistake' is a general word for any error, while 'malapropism' names a specific kind of error, with a word confused for another.
A spoonerism swaps sounds between words, while a malapropism substitutes a similar-sounding but wrong word.

examples.everyday: My dad always says 'a dull roar' when he means something else, and it's a funny malapropism every time.
examples.professional: In the code review, a colleague's malapropism about 'latency' and 'latitude' got us all laughing, but the meaning was clear.
examples.analytical: The comic effect of the malapropism depends on the audience recognizing both the intended word and the absurd substitute.

nuance.analogy: A malapropism is like a wrong key that almost opens the lock: the sound fits, but the meaning doesn't.
nuance.etymology: Named after Mrs. Malaprop, a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's play The Rivals (1775), who misuses big words; her name comes from French mal à propos, 'inappropriate.'
common_mistakes: Using 'malapropism' to mean any spelling error or typo; it refers only to a wrong word that sounds similar.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in 'mal-uh-PROP-iz-um'; the stress falls on MAL.

senses.definition: To be brave or tough enough to deal with something in a manner that is considered strong or manly.
senses.example: I was wondering when he would man up and marry that girl he knocked up.

senses.definition: To staff adequately; to staff up; to successfully fill all needed labor positions.
senses.example: We finally managed to man up the night shift after three weeks of posting job ads.

senses.definition: (Of personnel) to assemble, each person manning (attending to) his station, prepared for the departure of an aircraft, ship, etc.
senses.example: The crew was told to man up the destroyer for departure at dawn.

senses.definition: To vigorously guard the opponent to whom one is assigned.
senses.example: Our coach told the defenders to man up and stay tight on their assigned opponents.

core.definition: To show courage or toughness and face a difficult situation, often said to urge someone to stop complaining or avoiding a problem.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UP, the second word, and 'man' stays short and light. Do not stress 'man' or pronounce it as 'MAN-up' as a single compound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or confrontational. It can sound dismissive, rude or gender-stereotyped, especially when used to criticize someone's feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrasal verb informally among friends, coworkers or family, often as a mild or sometimes harsh demand to stop whining and face something. In professional settings it can sound unkind, so many people prefer 'step up' or 'own it.' The verb takes 'up to' when followed by an object, as in 'man up to the mistake.'

distinctions.note: Step up means to take responsibility or rise to a challenge, without the gender framing and with less harshness.
Buck up means to cheer up or take heart; man up is a demand to be tougher.
Toughen up is more neutral and usable for anyone; man up ties courage to masculinity.

examples.everyday: Stop complaining about the cold and man up; we still have two miles to hike.
examples.professional: Instead of hiding the missed deadline, you need to man up and tell the client what happened.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the phrase man up ties courage to masculinity, which makes it a poor description of what is really a virtue of honesty.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling on your boots before a hard hike: you do the uncomfortable part so the rest can go on.
nuance.etymology: Modern American phrasal verb from man (Old English mann) plus up; the courage sense is comparatively recent.
common_mistakes: Saying 'man up the problem' instead of 'man up to the problem'; the phrase needs 'to' before its object.
Using 'man up' in formal workplace writing, where 'take responsibility' or 'step up' is safer.

man-up.etymology: From *man* + *up*, with influence from *own up*, *buck up*.

senses.definition: By hand.
senses.example: stimulate someone manually

senses.definition: Using a human, as opposed to a computer.
senses.example: The student manually corrected several errors missed by the spell checker.

core.definition: By hand, or done by a person rather than automatically by a machine or computer program.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAN. The middle part is quick and reduced, and the final -ly is a clear lee, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is factual and used without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use manually often in technology and engineering, for example 'You have to reset it manually.' In everyday speech, by hand is more common, while manually sounds more formal or technical. It is often paired with automatically to contrast human control with machine control.

distinctions.note: By hand is more common in everyday speech, while manually sounds more technical or formal.

examples.everyday: The old thermostat has to be set manually every morning, so I just do it before I leave.
examples.professional: Please don't update the spreadsheet manually, because the script already handles it every night.
examples.analytical: The model's parameters were tuned manually, which makes its results hard to reproduce from the paper alone.

nuance.analogy: Manually is like steering a car by hand instead of letting the autopilot follow the road.
nuance.etymology: Manual from Latin manualis, 'of the hand', with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing manually with mentally, which has a different meaning
Pronouncing the final -ly as a long ee instead of a short lee

senses.definition: The transformation of raw materials into finished products, usually on a large scale.
The industry in which such products are made.
senses.example: Manufacturing employs nearly a tenth of the workers in our county.

senses.definition: Used in manufacturing.
senses.example: The manufacturing plant on Route 9 added a second shift this spring.

core.definition: The business of making products from raw materials, usually in factories and on a large scale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAK, with the first syllable lighter. The middle syllables are weak, and the final -ing is a short ing sound, not a long eeng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In American politics and news, it can carry strong feelings about jobs, decline or revival.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use manufacturing for the factory sector and for the process of making goods, as in 'She works in manufacturing.' It is also an adjective, as in manufacturing plant or manufacturing jobs. When people talk about the Rust Belt or reshoring, manufacturing is a loaded term tied to jobs and national identity.

distinctions.note: Production is broader and can include farming, film, software or services, while manufacturing specifically involves turning materials into finished goods.
Industry is a wider category that can include services, mining and agriculture, while manufacturing refers specifically to making products.

examples.everyday: My dad worked in manufacturing at a steel plant for thirty years before he retired.
examples.professional: Our manufacturing team cut the defect rate by a third this quarter by changing the inspection process.
examples.analytical: The long decline of manufacturing employment has reshaped politics across the Midwest in ways economists still debate.

nuance.analogy: Manufacturing is the factory's assembly line, where raw materials move from one station to another until they become finished products.
nuance.etymology: From manufacture plus the suffix -ing, from Latin manu factum, 'made by hand'.
common_mistakes: Using a manufacturing as a countable noun for a factory, when plant or factory is more natural
Stressing the wrong syllable, for example man-yoo-fack-TOOR-ing instead of man-yuh-FAK-chuh-ring

senses.definition: Someone who has control over something or someone.
The owner of an animal or slave.
senses.example: The horse's master whistled, and the animal trotted obediently back to the barn.

senses.definition: Someone who employs others.
An expert at something.
senses.example: Mark Twain was a master of fiction.

senses.definition: A tradesman who is qualified to teach apprentices.
senses.example: My grandfather apprenticed under a master carpenter who taught him to cut dovetail joints.

senses.definition: A skilled artist.
A master's degree; a type of postgraduate degree, usually undertaken after a bachelor degree.
senses.example: She has a master in psychology.

senses.definition: A person holding such a degree.
senses.example: He is a master of marine biology.

senses.definition: The original of a document or of a recording.
senses.example: The band couldn't find the master, so they re-recorded their tracks.

senses.definition: The primary wide shot of a scene, into which the closeups will be edited later.
senses.example: The director filmed a master shot of the whole wedding before moving in for closeups.

senses.definition: A parajudicial officer (such as a referee, an auditor, an examiner, or an assessor) specially appointed to help a court with its proceedings.
senses.example: The case was tried by a master, who concluded that the plaintiffs were the equitable owners of the property. […]

senses.definition: A device that is controlling other devices or is an authoritative source.
senses.example: a master wheel

senses.definition: A person holding an office of authority, especially the presiding officer.
senses.example: The master of the lodge called the meeting to order at seven o'clock sharp.

senses.definition: A person holding a similar office in other civic societies.
senses.example: The master of the Livery Company presided over the annual banquet in the guildhall.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of master key.
A male dominant.
senses.example: They negotiated a clear safe word before the scene, since the master wanted explicit consent.

senses.definition: The captain of a merchant ship; a master mariner.
senses.example: The master of the freighter radioed the port authority to report a broken rudder.

senses.definition: The copyright in a sound recording.
senses.example: Many modern recording artists value owning their masters.

senses.definition: A vessel having a specified number of masts.
senses.example: a two-master

senses.definition: (dated) A male head of household.
senses.example: In the old novel, the master of the house expected every servant to rise before dawn.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A male schoolteacher.
senses.example: Our village school had one master who taught reading, arithmetic, and Latin to every child.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A man or a boy; mister. See Master.
senses.example: Good morning, master, would you like your boots polished today?
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Masterful.
senses.example: a master performance

senses.definition: Main, principal or predominant.
senses.example: Our master plan for the campus focuses on sustainable housing and better transit.

senses.definition: Highly skilled.
senses.example: master batsman

senses.definition: Original.
senses.example: master copy

senses.definition: To be a master.
senses.example: Only after a decade of study did she truly master her craft.

senses.definition: To become the master of; to subject to one's will, control, or authority; to conquer; to overpower; to subdue.
senses.example: The army finally mastered the rebel province after a long and bloody campaign.

senses.definition: To learn to a high degree of proficiency.
senses.example: It took her years to master the art of needlecraft.

senses.definition: To make a master copy of.
senses.example: The studio mastered the album in Los Angeles before sending it to the pressing plant.

senses.definition: To earn a Master's degree.
senses.example: He mastered in English at the state college.

core.definition: A person who has control or authority over others, such as an owner; also a highly skilled expert in a craft.

pronunciation.tip: The first vowel is the short a of cat, not the o of cot. The final syllable is a reduced r-colored vowel, and the s and t are both clearly heard.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means a skilled expert or a degree, but negative when it refers to control over people, given the history of slavery in the United States.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use master in master's degree, master key, master plan and master of ceremonies. Many organizations now replace master bedroom, master bathroom and master/slave terms with primary, main, leader and follower or replica. In normal work talk, say boss or owner instead of master for a person in charge.

distinctions.note: An expert has deep knowledge; a master has reached a high level of skill and often a sense of command over the craft.
A boss is an everyday word for a supervisor or employer; master in the sense of owner is largely dated and harsh in modern speech.

examples.everyday: Tom's a master at fixing bikes, so he took a look at mine this weekend.
examples.professional: We need a master plan for the database migration before anyone touches production.
examples.analytical: The philosopher argues that a master of a practice differs from an expert in knowing why its rules work, not merely that they do.

nuance.analogy: A master is like a conductor who has memorized the score so well that the orchestra follows without visible effort.
nuance.etymology: From Old English mægester, from Latin magister 'teacher, chief'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in cot (MAH-ster); it is the short a of cat.
Using master for a boss or owner in everyday speech, which can sound harsh or offensive.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, master usually translates Greek kyrios (lord, master), which in the New Testament can refer to Jesus as Lord, and despotes (master, owner). Matthew 6:24 says that no one can serve two masters, and the point is that loyalty to God cannot be divided. Matthew 23:10 says that you have one master, the Christ, so the disciples' authority rests in Christ alone. Ephesians 6:9 tells earthly masters that they too have a Master in heaven, which shapes how they should treat those under them.

senses.definition: Used to say that a negative-containing statement of the previous speaker applies to the speaker as well.
senses.example: "I don't go there any more." / "Me neither."

core.definition: Used to agree with a negative statement a person just made, meaning 'I don't either' or 'I haven't either.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'NEE', and the 'th' in 'neither' is voiced, like the 'th' in 'the'. Many Americans also say 'NYE-dhur', so both pronunciations are fine.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'me neither' constantly in casual talk, such as 'I don't like cold weather.' 'Me neither.' Grammar teachers prefer 'Neither do I,' but 'me neither' is standard in everyday speech. A natural reply is 'Yeah, me neither' or 'Really? Me neither.'

distinctions.note: 'Me neither' agrees with a negative statement, while 'me too' agrees with a positive one.
'Neither do I' is grammatically preferred in formal writing and in grammar lessons, while 'me neither' is more common in speech.

examples.everyday: I never really liked horror movies. Me neither, they give me nightmares.
examples.professional: The client said they could not sign off on Friday, and I said, me neither, so we should move the review to next week.
examples.analytical: In the debate, she claimed the evidence did not support the policy, and he replied, me neither, which shifted the disagreement to the interpretation of the data.

nuance.analogy: 'Me neither' is a mirror: when someone says no, you say no too.
nuance.etymology: Combines the object pronoun 'me' with 'neither,' from Old English nawþer, meaning 'not either.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'me too' after a negative statement, which makes the agreement sound contradictory.
Pronouncing 'neither' with a hard 'th' as in 'thin'.

conversation.text: "I don't like cilantro." "Me neither. It tastes like soap."
"I've never seen snow." "Me neither!"
"I can't make it Friday." "Me neither. How about Saturday?"

senses.definition: The meadow pipit (Anthus pratensis).
senses.example: On our walk across the English moor, a meadowlark sang from the heather near the stream.

senses.definition: Any of several songbirds of the genera Sturnella and Leistes, native to the Americas.
senses.example: Early in the morning, a western meadowlark sang from the fence line of the prairie.

core.definition: A North American songbird with a yellow breast and black V-shaped marking, known for its loud, clear song.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MED, and make the second syllable 'oh' with a clear, rounded vowel. End with an r sound, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, associated with open fields, nature and pleasant sounds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meadowlark' mainly for the Western and Eastern meadowlarks, two grassland birds common across much of North America. Some older British usage applies it to the meadow pipit, so 'meadow pipit' is the safer term if you are talking about Europe. Americans often recognize the bird by its song and the yellow chest.

distinctions.note: A lark is a different bird family, the Alaudidae, while meadowlarks are in the blackbird family in North America; 'lark' alone usually means a skylark or a fun prank.
The meadow pipit is a European bird, sometimes called a meadowlark in British usage, while the American meadowlark is a different species.

examples.everyday: We heard a meadowlark singing from the fence post while we were hiking.
examples.professional: The park service survey counted meadowlarks along the restored prairie, which helps measure habitat recovery.
examples.analytical: The meadowlark's song has been studied as an example of learned regional variation, similar to dialects in human speech.

nuance.analogy: A meadowlark's song is like a clear morning bell rising over an open field.
nuance.etymology: From meadow and lark, from Old English lāwerce, 'lark'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the American meadowlark with the European meadow pipit, which is a different species.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'lock' rather than 'lark'; the vowel is more open and the r is pronounced.

senses.definition: Having meaning, significant.
senses.example: I think we made a meaningful contribution to this project today.

senses.definition: Full of implication; heavy with unstated meaning.
senses.example: "So you enjoyed yourself, did you," she said, with a meaningful smile.

core.definition: Important or significant; having real value, purpose, or effect, especially for a person's life or understanding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MEE. The final -ful is usually a syllabic l with no vowel, so say it as 'fuhl', not 'FULL'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as valuable or important, though it can sound abstract when used for vague or sentimental things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use meaningful for conversations, work, relationships, and experiences that matter to someone. In casual speech, 'That was meaningful' is a warm compliment. It is weaker than 'significant' when you need a measurable or statistical sense.

distinctions.note: Significant often means large, measurable, or statistically notable, while meaningful means it matters to a person or purpose.
Important says something deserves priority or attention, while meaningful says it has personal or deeper value.

examples.everyday: That talk with my dad about his job was really meaningful to me.
examples.professional: This project gives me meaningful work that our team can actually measure.
examples.analytical: For Kant, a life becomes meaningful when it is guided by principles that a rational agent can endorse.

nuance.analogy: A meaningful word is like a key that fits a lock: it connects to something real.
nuance.etymology: From meaning plus the suffix -ful, 'full of'; meaning comes from Old English mǣnan, 'to intend'.
common_mistakes: Using meaningful to mean 'meaningful' in the sense of 'useful', as in a meaningful tool; 'useful' or 'helpful' is often better.
Confusing meaningful with meaningless when stressing a contrast; check the prefix before answering.

senses.definition: The use of machinery to replace human or animal labor, especially in agriculture and industry.

core.definition: The replacement of human or animal labor with machines, especially in farming, mining and factories.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZAY, the fourth syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun'. Spell it with a z in American English, and say the first syllable as 'MEK'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest progress or job loss depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mechanization' mainly in history, economics, agriculture and manufacturing. It's not casual; in everyday talk people usually say 'machines' or 'automation'. In American English the spelling is with z, not the British 'mechanisation'.

distinctions.note: Mechanization replaces human muscle with machines, while automation means machines run with little or no human control.
Industrialization is the broad shift to factories and industry, while mechanization is the specific use of machinery to do work.

examples.everyday: The mechanization of the bakery's packing line means they need far fewer people on the night shift.
examples.professional: The mechanization of our warehouse cut picking costs by nearly half within a year.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that mechanization reshaped labor relations more profoundly than it reshaped production itself.

nuance.analogy: Mechanization is like swapping a hand-cranked mixer for an electric one: the work still gets done, but the machine now does the heavy lifting.
nuance.etymology: From mechanize, with the suffix -ation denoting a process.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'mechanisation'; Americans write 'mechanization'.
Confusing it with 'mechanic', the worker who repairs machines.

senses.definition: To melt fully, especially metal or glass so that it can be remade into something else.
To lose structure by being heated to a molten state.
senses.example: The reactor core melted down.

senses.definition: To have a breakdown; to collapse or fail utterly.

core.definition: To lose emotional control under stress and have a sudden outburst or collapse, often in public; also, of a system, to fail completely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DOWN, the particle, so melt is lighter. Say melt with a clear final t and link it smoothly into down, so the phrase sounds like melt-DOWN rather than two equal words.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a loss of control, though it is often said about children, stressed people or failing systems in a matter-of-fact way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to describe a toddler's tantrum, an adult's emotional outburst or a computer or plan that collapses. Casual reports such as 'He totally melted down' are common. A typical reply is 'Oh no, what happened?' or 'Take a breath, it's okay.'

distinctions.note: Lose it is more casual and often means getting angry; melt down suggests a collapse under sustained stress, often with tears or helplessness.
Break down is broader and can be neutral for cars or machines; melt down more strongly suggests a dramatic emotional or systemic collapse.

examples.everyday: The toddler melted down in the cereal aisle, so we left the cart and walked out.
examples.professional: The deployment melted down after the database hit its connection limit, so we rolled back the release.
examples.analytical: Under sustained moral scrutiny the institution did not reform gradually; it melted down, exposing decades of unacknowledged failure.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle left too close to a heater, a person or system that has been under heat too long suddenly gives way all at once.
nuance.etymology: From the verb melt (Old English meltan) plus the particle down; the breakdown sense is modern and informal.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb MELT instead of DOWN; the verb is melt DOWN, while the noun meltdown is MELT-down.
Using a transitive object with the breakdown sense: say 'he melted down', not 'he melted it down'. The metal sense, 'melt the metal down', is transitive.

senses.definition: A mechanical, thin, flat flexible part that can deform or vibrate when excited by an external force.
senses.example: The speaker's membrane vibrated so strongly that the bass notes rattled the cabinet.

senses.definition: A flexible or semiflexible covering or waterproofing whose primary function is to exclude water.
senses.example: We applied a waterproof membrane under the tile to keep moisture out of the basement wall.

senses.definition: A piece of parchment forming part of a roll.
senses.example: The medieval scribe copied the charter onto a membrane, one of many sheets in the roll.

senses.definition: A flexible enclosing or separating tissue forming a plane or film and separating two environments.
senses.example: The doctor explained that the thin membrane lining the lungs allows oxygen to pass into the blood.

senses.definition: A microscopic double layer of lipids and proteins forming the boundary of cells or organelles.
senses.example: Researchers found that the drug disrupts the lipid membrane surrounding the cancer cell.

core.definition: A thin, flexible layer of tissue or material that covers, lines or separates parts of a cell, organ or structure, letting some substances pass and blocking others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MEM. The 'e' in the first syllable is a short 'eh' sound, and the final 'ane' is a long 'ay' vowel followed by a clear American 'n'; do not add an extra vowel between 'm' and 'br'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'membrane' in everyday talk about biology and food, like 'the thin membrane around an egg' or 'cell membrane'. In construction, 'membrane' also names a waterproof roofing or pond liner, and in engineering it can mean a thin diaphragm that vibrates, as in a speaker or microphone.

distinctions.note: A film is a thin layer of any material on a surface, while a membrane is specifically a living or engineered barrier that selectively lets things through.
Skin is the outer organ of the body, while a membrane is an internal or thin covering that may be inside the body or in equipment.

examples.everyday: Peel the thin membrane off the orange before you eat the segments.
examples.professional: We need a waterproof membrane under the new roof, so the plan includes a layer of rubber sheeting.
examples.analytical: The cell membrane regulates what enters and leaves the cell, so its selective permeability is central to how cells maintain their internal balance.

nuance.analogy: A membrane is like a bouncer at a club: it lets some people through and stops others.
nuance.etymology: From Latin membrana, meaning a skin or thin covering.
common_mistakes: Saying 'MEM-brin' with a weak vowel in the first syllable.
Using 'membrane' for any thin layer, when a film or coating is often the better word.

membrane.etymology: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin *membrāna* (“skin or membrane that covers parts of the body”), from *membrum* + *-āna*.

senses.definition: A short note serving as a reminder.
senses.example: She left a memorandum on the fridge reminding everyone to take out the recycling.

senses.definition: A written business communication.
senses.example: The director sent a memorandum to all staff announcing the new remote work policy.

senses.definition: A brief diplomatic communication.
senses.example: The embassy delivered a memorandum protesting the new tariffs to the foreign ministry.

senses.definition: A page in an annual publication honoring the memory of a person who died during the past year.
senses.example: The yearbook included a memorandum page honoring the teacher who passed away last spring.

core.definition: A brief written message within an organization, used to inform, instruct, or record decisions for colleagues or staff.
